target: AG1’s claim that a national Election Day holiday would remove major schedule-based barriers by giving people time off from work and school
objection: A federal Election Day holiday would not legally require most private employers to close or provide paid time off, so many private-sector workers—especially in retail and service jobs—would still have to work or lose pay on Election Day.

target: AG1’s claim that a national holiday would remove the biggest scheduling barriers for millions of Americans, including workers
objection: The workers most constrained by schedules are often low-income workers with less flexibility and less ability to absorb lost wages, so the people facing the biggest barriers would still be affected even if Election Day were a holiday.

target: AG1’s claim that an Election Day holiday is a good turnout strategy
objection: Research indicates that making Election Day a holiday by itself is not an effective way to increase voter turnout compared with other voting-access reforms, so it is a weak or unreliable strategy on its own.

target: AG2’s objection that private employers are not required to give paid time off or close, so a holiday would have little effect
objection: Even without a legal mandate on private employers, a national holiday typically changes workplace and community scheduling practices in ways that create more workable time windows for voting, so it can still produce meaningful flexibility.

target: AG2’s objection that remaining barriers for some workers mean the policy should be rejected
objection: A policy can still be justified if it removes major schedule barriers for millions of people, even if it does not solve every barrier for every worker.

target: AG2’s claim that low-income workers would still be blocked because the holiday does not guarantee paid time off
objection: For many parents, the key obstacle is coordinating voting with children’s school or daycare schedules; a national holiday would often alter those schedules and create more feasible daytime voting opportunities, so it would directly help many low-income workers, especially parents.

target: AG2’s claim that a federal holiday is not broadly workable or legitimate
objection: The proposal is broadly supported by majorities of Democrats and Republicans and is consistent with the practice of many OECD countries, so it is workable and legitimate rather than unusual or impractical.

target: AG2’s claim that a holiday would not help because employers are not legally required to provide paid time off
objection: Holiday status changes social expectations; workers are less likely to face job-related penalties for taking time to vote on a holiday than on an ordinary weekday, so the holiday can reduce a real work-related barrier even without guaranteed paid leave.

target: AG2’s claim that a holiday is not a reliable turnout strategy because it depends on whether private employers provide paid time off
objection: Even when it is not the single most effective turnout reform, a holiday can still increase turnout by elevating civic importance and changing how people plan for voting, so it is not inherently an unreliable mechanism.

target: AG2’s claim that holiday status would not meaningfully expand working voters’ access windows because employers may stay open and polling hours stay the same
objection: A national holiday can still reduce the time cost of voting by shifting commutes and public schedules toward weekend or holiday patterns, and election administrators may adjust polling hours or staffing, creating more practical voting opportunities.

target: AG2’s claim that voting access depends mainly on whether employers are legally required to provide paid time off
objection: The practical barrier is not only paid leave; it is also the time cost of leaving work, traveling, waiting, and voting during fixed polling hours. A holiday can reduce that time cost even without universal paid closure.

target: AG1’s claim that a federal holiday creates workable time windows and reduces barriers for many voters
objection: Because federal holiday status does not require most private employers to close or give paid time off, the real benefit is uneven and employer-dependent rather than guaranteed for all employees.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday removes major barriers for low-income workers and parents
objection: Low-income workers are more likely to have inflexible private-sector jobs, and holiday status alone may not eliminate the need to staff those shifts, so many still would have work hours overlapping polling hours.

target: AG1’s claim that holiday status meaningfully expands access windows because people can vote around work shifts
objection: If workers still must work during specified polling hours and polling hours do not automatically expand, then holiday status does not reliably expand practical voting windows for them.

target: AG1’s claim that holiday status would directly address the biggest constraints for low-income parents by improving school/daycare availability
objection: A federal holiday does not uniformly require schools or childcare providers to close or align schedules in a way that helps parents vote, and parents may still need alternative supervision that is costly or unavailable, so the holiday does not reliably solve that childcare barrier.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday is a reliable national strategy for low-income parents
objection: If a policy does not reliably remove the main practical barriers for low-income parents, then it is a poor national solution; a holiday by itself does not reliably improve childcare or supervision during polling hours.

target: AG1’s claim that a federal holiday reliably guarantees workers time to vote
objection: A federal Election Day holiday does not legally require most private employers to close or provide paid time off, so workers’ ability to vote remains employer-dependent rather than guaranteed.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday would reliably remove major voting-access barriers for low-income workers
objection: Research shows that an election holiday by itself is not an effective turnout-increase strategy, especially because it does not reliably fix the wage-loss and job-risk constraints faced by low-income workers.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday reduces time-cost enough to solve scheduling barriers for low-income workers
objection: For many low-income workers in inflexible service and retail jobs, holiday status does not eliminate overlapping work shifts or the need to miss paid work during polling hours.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday’s civic-framing effects can overcome access problems
objection: Making voting feel more civic-minded may increase motivation, but if workers still cannot get practical time away from fixed shifts, increased motivation does not remove the binding time constraint.

target: AG1’s claim that holiday-related commuting changes reduce travel friction and expand access windows
objection: Holiday schedules can actually make public transit and related services run on reduced or modified schedules, so a holiday does not reliably reduce travel-time or access friction for working and low-income voters.

target: AG1’s claim that a federal holiday meaningfully removes scheduling barriers for low-income voters
objection: If holiday effects depend on employer discretion rather than enforceable rights, then access remains uneven and employer-dependent instead of reliably improved for the voters most constrained by schedules.

target: AG1’s claim that a national holiday is the best national approach to election access
objection: A reform that does not reliably remove the biggest scheduling barriers for low-income voters should not be the national solution when more reliable alternatives exist, such as enforceable state time-off rules and automatic voter registration.

target: AG1’s claim that holiday status will reduce total time-on-task for voters
objection: In-person voting includes queue and wait time, and a holiday can increase same-day turnout demand without automatically increasing polling capacity, so total time-on-task may stay the same or worsen rather than reliably fall.

target: AG1’s claim that public support and OECD examples show the holiday is workable and legitimate
objection: Broad public support and the fact that some OECD countries hold elections on weekends or holidays do not prove that a standalone U.S. federal holiday would reliably give constrained workers enforceable time to vote.

target: AG1’s claim that a federal holiday reliably guarantees voting time without wage loss or job risk
objection: Because most private employers are not legally required to close or provide paid time off, a federal holiday does not reliably guarantee constrained workers compensated time to vote.
